title: Anticipating confusion
content:
I know that _you_ know that taking this exit will get us to Sheridan Drive, but the person who’s likely to be driving down this road in a few minutes has no idea.

Let’s agree that most street signs are for folks who know where they’re going. We would label things differently if we were instructing those that don’t.

I know that you know that ERASE isn’t the same thing as DELETE, but the next person interacting with your command-line interface might not know.

Of course this is obvious when we say it so clearly. And yet, there are many kinds of USB cables, poorly named and labeled. The instructions that come with just about anything we buy were written by lawyers for juries, not by a product manager who actually wanted to inform and delight.

Design to be understood. And design so that the inevitable confusion of the newbie doesn’t get worse. Because without your active intervention, it will.

title: Americans Who Go to Church and Trust Science Are Also More Likely to Believe in Ghosts and Curses
content:
Americans who trust science and reason more than their churches’ teachings, but still believe in God or attend services, are also more likely to believe in magic than those who prioritize religious teachings.

This was the central finding of a study my co-authors and [I](https://www.american.edu/spa/faculty/rli.cfm) published in the journal [_Social Forces_](https://doi.org/10.1093/sf/soag097) in July 2026. We analyzed the latest wave of the [Baylor Religion Survey](https://baylorreligionsurvey.research.baylor.edu/), a nationally representative survey of 1,812 American adults that [Gallup](https://www.gallup.com/home.aspx) fielded in early 2025.

We used four of its questions to measure an outlook we call “secular rationalism.” The term refers to the belief that science is the only way to understand the world and that morality should rest on reason rather than religious teachings. Secular rationalism also includes the idea that people should interpret spiritual matters on their own rather than trust religious authorities.

We looked at people who embrace secular rationalist ideas but also believe in the supernatural. We asked respondents how strongly they believed in six things that people often call magic and require no god or church, from ghosts and curses to talking to the dead. For comparison, we also measured belief in miracles, such as whether miracles still happen today and whether God is the source of all miracles.

What’s interesting was that people who scored high on “secular rationalism” beliefs were more likely to believe in magic, so long as they kept some tie to religion. Among Americans who believe in God, those who also agree with secular rationalism were about twice as likely to lean toward magic as those who reject secular rationalism – 40% vs. 19%. Among people who attend religious services, the share was 28% vs. 19%. Among people who never attend services or do not believe in God, secular rationalism was no longer linked to belief in magic.

Some of the groups we compared were small. According to Baylor Religion Survey 2025 data, fewer than 1% of Americans neither believe in God nor generally agree with these secular rationalist ideas but actively reject them, while about 18% believe in God and agree with them.

**Why It Matters**

About 3 in 10 American adults now claim [no religious affiliation](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/decline-of-christianity-in-the-us-has-slowed-may-have-leveled-off/). Scholars are still debating whether the decline of organized religion will also mean the [decline of belief in the supernatural](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/why-religion-went-obsolete-9780197800737?cc=us&lang=en&) in the U.S. A long tradition of social theory predicts that as religious institutions decline, a [scientific outlook with no room](https://sociology.sas.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/Weber-Science-as-a-Vocation.pdf) for supernatural or magic will take its place.

Our findings suggest that many Americans who no longer affiliate with an organized religion may still believe in tarot, astrology or psychic services. More broadly, most Americans without a religion still hold some spiritual belief. [According to the Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/religious-and-spiritual-beliefs/), 29% of Americans have no religion, but only 5% call themselves atheists. Most say their religion is “nothing in particular,” and two-thirds of that group still believe in something beyond the natural world.

Why are we seeing this trend? As French sociologist Emile Durkheim wrote in 1912, “[The magician has a clientele, not a church](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/41360).” Magic needs no congregation, clergy or theology, so believers can adopt it without leaving their church. That makes magic a natural fit for people who still believe in God but no longer let institutions define the supernatural for them. It may also explain its appeal to younger Americans, who [distrust institutions most](https://doi.org/10.1162/daed_a_01943) and, as our data suggests, are likely to believe in both magic and secular rationalism.

**What’s Next**

Our data comes from a single point in time. It shows that people who are religious but also trust science and reason are more likely to believe in magic. But it can’t tell us whether these people are drifting away from religion, coming back to it or staying where they are. To find out, we would need to survey the same people who participated in the original survey over time.

Archaeologist [Chris Gosden](https://www.arch.ox.ac.uk/people/professor-chris-gosden) argues that belief in [magic is older](https://academic.macmillan.com/academictrade/9781250800152/magicahistory/) than both religion and science, and for most of history it has existed side by side with religion. What our study adds is a clearer picture of when trust in science goes hand in hand with magic: among people who stay religious but no longer let their church decide what is true.

We still know little about how magical beliefs spread among young Americans, or why they appeal to them. Answering those questions is an important next step for research on belief. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Can We Ditch BMI for an Obesity Index That Predicts Disease Risk Better?
content:
As far as obesity measures go, body mass index leaves a lot to be desired. It’s ridiculously simplistic, taking into account just two measurements: height and weight. It also doesn’t account for things like fat distribution, muscle mass, or other metrics known to influence health.

On the other hand, this simplicity makes it incredibly convenient. Combine that with research continuity and inertia (BMI has been around for almost two centuries), and you can see why we haven’t been able to ditch it. But what if there are better obesity indices out there, ones with more predictive power when it comes to disease risk? That’s the question that a study newly published in _Science Bulletin_ is asking.

**Read more: “[Fat Cells May Retain a Memory of Obesity](https://nautil.us/fat-cells-may-retain-a-memory-of-obesity-1285557)”**

To find an answer, a team of Chinese medical researchers analyzed health data from 4,258,033 adults between the ages of 35 and 75 years from the ChinaHEART cohort. The team compared 15 obesity indices belonging to three major groups—body shape, visceral fat, and metabolic function—examining how they were linked to major chronic diseases.

In general, higher values for most of the indices were associated with higher risks of cardiovascular disease and diabetes, but relationships to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and cancer were weaker (in fact, some indices showed nonlinear or even inverse associations with these illnesses). Taken together, the results suggest that the full range of obesity-related health risks likely can’t be captured by a single measure.

The team then investigated how well each index could distinguish individuals at different levels of risk for chronic diseases. Here, too they found plenty of variability. For example, the Chinese visceral adiposity index (an estimate of body fat) was better at predicting risk of cardiovascular disease, while the triglyceride-glucose index (a measure of metabolic function) was better at predicting diabetes risk.

Interestingly, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease risk was best predicted by a body shape index. This metric measures the proportion of abdominal fat to size and is usually used to estimate the risk of premature mortality, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. It makes sense when you consider fat distribution can also affect respiratory function.

Cancer was an outlier. According to the team, none of the obesity metrics they studied showed a strong association with the disease. Then again, the relationships they found for other diseases were moderate at best, and that’s not the only caveat. Because the cohort members were all from mainland China, the researchers warn that their results may not apply to other ethnicities.

In other words, we may be stuck with the simplistic yet convenient BMI for quite some time. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Celebrating 20 Years of The Marginalian and the Search for Meaning: Free Livestream This Friday

### By Maria Popova

At the dawn of my twenties, lonely, destitute, and disoriented by the demands of making a new life in an alien world, I started keeping notes on my search for meaning while working four jobs to pay my way through college. On October 23, 2006, I began sharing my discoveries — passages from books, links to neuroscience studies, reproductions of 16th-century Japanese woodcuts — in an office email to seven colleagues. They in turn began sharing it with friends, who began sharing it with friends. The fractal spread and, within a few years, the Library of Congress had included it in its permanent digital archive of culturally valuable materials. It changed shape (the essays grew longer, the questions deeper) and name ([_Brain Pickings_ became _The Marginalian_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/)) but continued beating with the same heart, reckoning with the ongoing bewilderment of being alive — sometimes through science and philosophy, sometimes through poetry and children’s books, always through the lens of wonder, always offered freely: no advertising, no AI, not even an assistant, a thoroughly one-woman labor of love sustained by the love of strangers.

To [celebrate](https://spac.org/events/constellating-wonder/) twenty years of it, I am inviting friends from various walks of life — poets and physicists, musicians and actors, artists and historians of science — to read fragments of the writings, poetry and prose, that have most touched me over the years as I introduce each with a short reflection on its resonance to the eternal questions we live with: what do we make of our suffering, why did the world have to be beautiful, how do we see more clearly and love more purely.

With the format of [_The Universe in Verse_](https://www.themarginalian.org/the-universe-in-verse/) and the feeling-tone of my _Marginalian_ essays, the evening will feature live appearances and special contributions across spacetime by a constellation of beloved humans who have made my own life more livable over the years, among them Debbie Millman, Joan As Police Woman, Krista Tippett, Marie Howe, Diane Ackerman, James Gleick, Natascha McElhone, Sophie Blackall, Stephon Alexander, Natalie Batalha, Willow Defebaugh, Wendy MacNaughton, Zoë Keating, Nick Cave, Paola Prestini with the Young People’s Chorus of New York City, and surprise guests.

# The Map to the Route of Your Life

### By Maria Popova

No one will map for you the path by which you must cross the wilderness of your own life — not your parents or your teachers, not your heroes or your lovers, not the self-help books or Shakespeare’s sonnets. Some may give you signposts, some may become turning points, but it is a path you ultimately make by walking. Along the way, you mistake dreams and desires for destinations, only to find that they have been way-stations — as soon as you attain them, you begin longing for something else. This Möbius strip of longing is the root of everything we suffer in the fangs of [the Wanting Monster](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/05/29/the-wanting-monster/), but it is also the root of our creative vitality: the restless urge to make, to leave a mark that says “I AM,” a monument to having been. It is our incompleteness that maps the territory of the possible in us. It is our existential wanderlust that makes us what we are — pilgrims of mortality, forever coming home to the horizon of tomorrow.

[Mario Benedetti](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/mario-benedetti/) (September 14, 1920–May 17, 2009) captures this paradox, with subtlety that doesn’t offer an answer but whispers the living question back to you, in an unedited poem found among his papers after his death, beautifully read in the original Spanish by my Patagonian friend [Manuel Gutiérrez](https://www.instagram.com/mamogutierrez/) — a communicator of wonder through theater, music, and humor, whose hospitality made the [serpentine birdworlds](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/07/27/serpentine-birdworlds/) possible and who is always teaching me how to navigate the terrain of life with an open heart for a compass.

> el piélago de antes ya no estaba  
>  todo era más fuerte más seguro  
>  de pronto me encontré con la ribera  
>  de ese río que siempre fue mi anhelo
> 
> 
> sólo entonces me aconsejé a mí mismo  
>  en el bolsillo volví a poner la ruta  
>  y allí quedó esperando  
>  otro mañana

> **ROADMAP**  
> _by Mario Benedetti_  
> _translated by Maria Popova_
> 
> 
> I found it in my pocket / it was a roadmap  
>  I knew not where it led  
>  but I followed it anyway in aimless wanderlust  
>  with all my nostalgias in hand
> 
> 
> it was an atlas of the soul / of consciousness  
>  of what I have committed and what awaits me  
>  on the ground I saw footprints that were my own  
>  and so it was a path already trodden
> 
> 
> the vastness of before had vanished  
>  everything was stronger, surer  
>  suddenly I landed on the riverbank  
>  the river that had always been my longing
> 
> 
> only then did I heed my own advice  
>  I tucked the path into my pocket once more  
>  and there it remained, awaiting  
>  another tomorrow

Couple with Benedetti’s [clarion call to stop waiting and start living](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/01/10/no-te-salves/), then revisit C.S. Lewis on [what we long for in our existential longings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/09/03/c-s-lewis-longing/).

# Bloom: A Touching Animated Short Film about Depression and What It Takes to Recover the Light of Being

### By Maria Popova

“Sometimes one has simply to endure a period of depression for what it may hold of illumination if one can live through it, attentive to what it exposes or demands,” the poet May Sarton wrote as she contemplated [the cure for despair](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/10/17/may-sarton-journal-of-a-solitude-depression/) amid a dark season of the spirit. But what does it take to perch that precarious _if_ in the direction of the light? When we are in that dark and hollow place, that place of leaden loneliness and isolation, when “the gray drizzle of horror induced by depression takes on the quality of physical pain,” as William Styron wrote in his [classic account](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/09/depression-william-styron-darkness-visible/) of the malady — an indiscriminate malady that [savaged Keats](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/06/13/keats-depression/) and [savaged Nietzsche](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/02/12/nietzsche-hope/) and [savaged Hansberry](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/07/lorraine-hansberry-depression/) — what does it take to live through the horror and the hollowness to the other side, to look back and gasp disbelievingly, with the poet Jane Kenyon: [“What hurt me so terribly… until this moment?”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/09/27/having-it-out-with-melancholy-jane-kenyon-amanda-palmer/)

During a recent dark season of the spirit, a dear friend buoyed me with the most wonderful, hope-giving, rehumanizing story: Some years earlier, when a colleague of hers — another physicist — was going through such a season of his own, she gave him an amaryllis bulb in a small pot; the effect it had on him was unexpected and profound, as the effect of uncalculated kindnesses always is — profound and far-reaching, the way a pebble of kindness ripples out widening circles of radiance. As the light slowly returned to his life, he decided to teach a class on the physics of animation. And so it is that one of his students, Emily Johnstone, came to make _Bloom —_ a touching animated short film, drawing from the small personal gesture a universal metaphor for how we survive our densest private darknesses, consonant with Neil Gaiman’s insistence that [“sometimes it only takes a stranger, in a dark place… to make us warm in the coldest season.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/01/08/what-you-need-to-be-warm-neil-gaiman/)

[Video 3](https://vimeo.com/29865151)

Complement with Tim Ferriss on [how he survived suicidal depression](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/12/08/tim-ferriss-tools-of-titans-depression/) and Tchaikovsky on [depression and finding beauty amid the wreckage of the soul](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/11/19/tchaikovsky-letters-depession/), then revisit [“Having It Out with Melancholy”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/09/27/having-it-out-with-melancholy-jane-kenyon-amanda-palmer/) — Jane Kenyon’s stunning poem about life with and after depression.

# The Single Most Effective Remedy for Despair: Advice from T.H. White’s Merlyn

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 34: The Single Most Effective Remedy for Despair: Advice from T.H. White’s Merlyn](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/TheOnceAndFutureKing_white.jpg?fit=320%2C516&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Once-Future-King-T-White/dp/0441627404/?tag=braipick-20)

In his wonderful contribution to [_A Velocity of Being: Letters to a Young Reader_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/11/20/a-velocity-of-being-letters-to-a-young-reader/), Yo-Yo Ma tells children about how books helped him survive his own childhood, listing King Arthur among his three great heroes; as a young boy born in France to Chinese parents, trying to find his mooring as an immigrant in America, he reaped great consolation and inspiration from the tales of the legendary medieval leader — stories of “adventure, heroism, human frailty and accidental destiny” that emboldened him to believe in the power of the quest for holy grails and improbable dreams — dreams as improbable as a small boy with no homeland growing up to be the world’s greatest cellist.

And, indeed, buried inside the adventure-thrill of these Arthurian tales are treasure troves of wisdom on fortitude, courage, and the art of honorable living, nowhere richer than in the novels by **T.H. White** (May 29, 1906–January 17, 1964), one particular passage in which offers a meta-testament to the potency of reading in the character-formation of King Arthur himself.

[![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/CindyDerby.jpg?resize=680%2C918&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/a-velocity-of-being-cindy-derby_print?curator=brainpicker)

Art by Cindy Derby from [_A Velocity of Being: Letters to a Young Reader_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/11/20/a-velocity-of-being-letters-to-a-young-reader/). Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/a-velocity-of-being-cindy-derby_print?curator=brainpicker), benefitting the New York public library system.

In White’s 1958 Arthurian classic [**_The Once and Future King_**](https://www.amazon.com/Once-Future-King-T-White/dp/0441627404/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://www.worldcat.org/title/once-and-future-king/oclc/1037236469&referer=brief_results)) — one of Ursula K. Le Guin’s lifelong favorite books — the mystic-magician Merlyn, aware of the young not-yet-king Arthur’s destiny, endeavors to sculpt the boy’s moral fiber and to teach him what it means to be a strong, kindly leader through a series of lessons from the animal kingdom, transforming him by turns into a fish, a hawk, an ant, a goose, and a badger. One day, the young Arthur comes to Merlyn in his ordinary human incarnation, sulking with an ordinary human disappointment — that small, merciless mallet for our fragility. Merlyn offers his advice on the mightiest antidote to disappointment and sorrow:

> The best thing for being sad… is to learn something. That is the only thing that never fails. You may grow old and trembling in your anatomies, you may lie awake at night listening to the disorder of your veins, you may miss your only love, you may see the world about you devastated by evil lunatics, or know your honor trampled in the sewers of baser minds. There is only one thing for it then — to learn. Learn why the world wags and what wags it. That is the only thing which the mind can never exhaust, never alienate, never be tortured by, never fear or distrust, and never dream of regretting.

In a sentiment evocative of trailblazing astronomer Maria Mitchell’s observation that [“we have a hunger of the mind which asks for knowledge of all around us, and the more we gain, the more is our desire,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/06/05/maria-mitchell-science-religion/) Merlyn adds:

> Look at what a lot of things there are to learn — pure science, the only purity there is. You can learn astronomy in a lifetime, natural history in three, literature in six. And then, after you have exhausted a million lifetimes in biology and medicine and theocriticism and geography and history and economics — why, you can start to make a cartwheel out of the appropriate wood, or spend fifty years learning to begin to learn to beat your adversary at fencing. After that you can start again on mathematics, until it is time to learn to plough.

Complement with Rebecca Solnit — a modern-day magician of storytelling — on [how books solace, empower, and transform us](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/01/03/a-velocity-of-being-rebecca-solnit/), philosopher Martha Nussbaum on [how to live with our human fragility](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/03/14/martha-nussbaum-bill-moyers-world-of-ideas/), and poet Mary Oliver on [the greatest antidote to sorrow](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/11/02/mary-oliver-upstream-staying-alive-reading/), then revisit Bruce Lee’s [philosophy of learning](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/08/26/bruce-lee-learning/), Lewis Carroll’s [four rules of learning](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/06/13/how-to-learn-lewis-carroll/), and Albert Einstein’s advice to his own young son on [the secret to learning anything](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/06/14/einstein-letter-to-son/).

title: How to Hold Your Helplessness: Nobel Laureate Bertrand Russell’s Salve for the Anxiety of Overwhelm
content:
[![Image 1: How to Hold Your Helplessness: Nobel Laureate Bertrand Russell’s Salve for the Anxiety of Overwhelm](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/newhopesforachangingworld_TheMarginalian.jpg?fit=320%2C499&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Hopes-Changing-World-Bertrand-Russell/dp/9383723475/?tag=braipick-20)

“To be a good human being is to have a kind of openness to the world, an ability to trust uncertain things beyond your own control,” philosopher Martha Nussbaum concluded in considering [how to live with our human fragility](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/03/14/martha-nussbaum-bill-moyers-world-of-ideas/). And yet in the face of overwhelming uncertainty, when the world seems to splinter and crumble in the palm of our civilization’s hand, something deeper and more robust than blind trust is needed to keep us anchored to our own goodness — something pulsating with [rational faith in the human spirit](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/04/04/erich-fromm-anatomy-of-human-destructiveness/) and [a profound commitment to goodness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/03/30/iris-murdoch-against-the-gods/).

That is what [Bertrand Russell](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/bertrand-russell/) (May 18, 1872–February 2, 1970) explores in the out-of-print treasure [**_New Hopes for a Changing World_**](https://www.amazon.com/Hopes-Changing-World-Bertrand-Russell/dp/9383723475/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://www.worldcat.org/title/2828744)), composed a year after he [received the Nobel Prize](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/21/bertrand-russell-nobel-prize-acceptance-speech/), while humanity was still shaking off the dust and dread of its Second World War and already shuddering with the catastrophic nuclear threat of the Cold War.

[![Image 2: bertrandrussell3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/bertrandrussell3.jpg?resize=680%2C357&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Hopes-Changing-World-Bertrand-Russell/dp/9383723475/?tag=braipick-20)

Bertrand Russell

Observing that his time, like ours, is marked by “a feeling of impotent perplexity” and “a deep division in our souls between the sane and the insane parts,” Russell considers the consequence such total world-overwhelm has on the human spirit:

> One of the painful things about our time is that those who feel certainty are stupid, and those with any imagination and understanding are filled with doubt and indecision.

And yet, with his unfaltering reasoned optimism, he insists that there is an alternate view of our human destiny — one that vitalizes rather than paralyzes, based on “the completest understanding of the moods, the despairs, and the maddening doubts” that beset us; one that helps mitigate the worst of Western culture — “our restlessness, our militarism, our fanaticism, and our ruthless belief in mechanism” — and amplifies the best in it: “the spirit of free inquiry, the understanding of the conditions of general prosperity, and emancipation from superstition.” He examines the root of our modern perplexity, perhaps even more pronounced in our time than it was in his:

> Traditional systems of dogma and traditional codes of conduct have not the hold that they formerly had. Men and women are often in genuine doubt as to what is right and what is wrong, and even as to whether right and wrong are anything more than ancient superstitions. When they try to decide such questions for themselves they find them too difficult. They cannot discover any clear purpose that they ought to pursue or any clear principle by which they should be guided. Stable societies may have principles that, to the outsider, seem absurd. But so long as the societies remain stable their principles are subjectively adequate. That is to say they are accepted by almost everybody unquestioningly, and they make the rules of conduct as clear and precise as those of the minuet or the heroic couplet. Modern life, in the West, is not at all like a minuet or a heroic couplet. It is like free verse which only the poet can distinguish from prose.

[![Image 3](https://i1.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/margaretcook_leavesofgrass19.jpg?resize=768%2C973&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/i-will-confront-these-shows-of-the-day-and-night_framed-print?sku=s6-8968158p21a12v52a13v54?curator=brainpicker)

Illustration by Margaret C. Cook for a [rare 1913 edition of _Leaves of Grass_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/04/11/leaves-of-grass-margaret-cook/). (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/i-will-confront-these-shows-of-the-day-and-night_framed-print?sku=s6-8968158p21a12v52a13v54?curator=brainpicker).)

This torment, Russell argues, is simply the growing pains of our civilization. When we reach maturity, we would attain a life “full of joy and vigour and mental health.” Building on his lifelong reckoning with [the meaning of the good life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/05/18/bertrand-russell-what-i-believe-love/) and [the nature of happiness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/02/21/bertrand-russell-happiness/), he writes:

> The good life, as I conceive it, is a happy life. I do not mean that if you are good you will be happy; I mean that if you are happy you will be good. Unhappiness is deeply implanted in the souls of most of us.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> A way of life cannot be successful so long as it is a mere intellectual conviction. It must be deeply felt, deeply believed, dominant even in dreams.

He offers a lucid and luminous prescription for attaining the good life, individually and as a society:

> What I should put in the place of an ethic in the old sense is encouragement and opportunity for all the impulses that are creative and expansive. I should do everything possible to liberate men from fear, not only conscious fears, but the old imprisoned primeval terrors that we brought with us out of the jungle. I should make it clear, not merely as an intellectual proposition, but as something that the heart spontaneously believes, that it is not by making others suffer that we shall achieve our own happiness, but that happiness and the means to happiness depend upon harmony with other men. When all this is not only understood but deeply felt, it will be easy to live in a way that brings happiness equally to ourselves and to others. If men could think and feel in this way, not only their personal problems, but all the problems of world politics, even the most abstruse and difficult, would melt away. Suddenly, as when the mist dissolves from a mountain top, the landscape would be visible and the way would be clear. It is only necessary to open the doors of our hearts and minds to let the imprisoned demons escape and the beauty of the world take possession.

Complement [**_New Hopes for a Changing World_**](https://www.amazon.com/Hopes-Changing-World-Bertrand-Russell/dp/9383723475/?tag=braipick-20) with the poetic scientist Lewis Thomas on [how to live with ourselves and each other](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/03/02/the-fragile-species-lewis-thomas/) and Virginia Woolf on [finding beauty in the uncertainty of time, space, and being](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/04/03/virginia-woolf-to-the-lighthouse/), then revisit Russell on [the four desires driving all human behavior](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/21/bertrand-russell-nobel-prize-acceptance-speech/) and [how to grow old](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/07/03/how-to-grow-old-bertrand-russell/).

title: When The Present Eats The Future
content:
Credits

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

The Achilles heel of consumer democracies is that there is precious little constituency for the future in the present. All the feedback signals — in politics, culture and the market — are geared to short-term gratification. In each case, the incentives of the system deliver what the most influential demographic wants, and when they want it, which is now.

From fast fashion to electoral contests to quarterly earnings reports, the system is responsive to the pursuit of happiness defined by the near horizon.

The consequence of this, which Harvard sociologist Daniel Bell argued more than half a century ago in his book, “The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism,” is that the present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society. The recent Noema essay by Simon Curtis and Ian Klaus titled [“Americans Are Losing The Long Game”](https://www.noemamag.com/americans-are-losing-the-long-game/) is excellent on this point.

While state-guided _dirigiste_ policies that champion and support strategic industries deemed critical for the future are roundly frowned upon in market economies, the opposite rigidity of the short-term consumerist mentality is less appreciated as a critical failure of good governance. Yet, unless societies prepare for, subsidize and invest in the kind of future they want, they will never get there.

> “The present ends up eating the future to the detriment of the long-term sustainability of society.”

## **China’s Market-State Modality**

Of all the major powers, post-Mao China stands out in taking control of its future without sacrificing the present. Over recent decades, it has both lifted hundreds of millions into general prosperity while, at the same time, swiftly conquering the key industries of a sustainable future, from green technology to artificial intelligence.

One has to admit that the Middle Kingdom’s mix of a long-term planning framework checked by robust market signals and bolstered by strategically deployed subsidies has worked. Indeed, it has worked too well: Its overproduction is spilling out and flooding world markets, threatening to displace domestic jobs and industry elsewhere.

China has not arrived at this point overnight. It has been a long time coming. In 1987, the ideology chief of the Communist Party politburo at the time, Hu Qili, told me in Beijing: “The market is not a feature unique to capitalism. Capitalism does not have the patent right over the market economy. What we are trying to create is a new and unprecedented modality where planning is combined with the commodity economy, where the state regulates the market, and the market guides the enterprises.”

The overall economy is steered by a one-party political system designed to reach consensus over long-term goals that have the decisive thrust to be carried out over many years without a break in continuity. Once set, the policy path is followed with relative discipline by a leadership and administration that, while not based on popular appeal to an electorate, is systemically accountable for realizing its set objectives.

When a key strategic goal is ordained by the Party, the state fosters a “whole dragon” approach in which start-up subsidies, sourcing, supply chains and production capacity are vertically aligned, making it one of the most powerful production ensembles in economic history.

## **Flaws Linked To Strength**

The chief flaw of China’s system, of course, is closely linked to its strength. To keep the consensus from fraying, it overcompensates on the side of repressive order and control of freedom. It is the opposite of the open societies of the West, where the flaw lies within the strength of diverse participation and electoral competition: a growing inability to forge a consensus on long-term goals out of the cacophony of voices, the welter of contending interests and the immediate wash of fickle public opinion.

When all-out competitive partisanship destroys consensus among the body politic, the democratic transfer of power can mean a complete rupture of policies endorsed by most voters only four years earlier. Sticking to the course for the time it takes to reach fruition is not a reliable feature of this system.

The extreme edge of this stark difference can be seen in the contrasting behavior of the current leadership in the U.S. and China. America’s leader relishes dominating the memes of the moment, battling his way through every 24-hour news cycle by firing off social media barrages at sundry foes. China’s near-dictatorial leader has used his amassed clout to chart out a roadmap for the next half century.

## **China’s Long March To Owning Green Technologies**

Meeting in Mexico in 2012, the G-20 decided for the first time to put climate change on the agenda. In those days, the Berggruen Institute’s 21 st Century Council, a group of former heads of state and government, tech leaders and Nobel laureates, would meet with the chair of the G-20 each year to advise on its agenda.

That year’s chair, then Mexican president Felipe Calderón, invited the council for lunch in the garden of Los Pinos, the presidential palace, to discuss the upcoming meeting. When the topic turned to climate, Wu Jianmin, a top Chinese diplomat and executive director of the China Institute for Innovation and Development Strategy, related that a top priority of the then incoming Party leadership of Xi Jinping would be “ecological civilization.”

All those 14 years ago, he confidently laid out a trajectory of China’s decisive shift to electric vehicles and plans for massive R&D investment in battery storage for wind and solar as well as EVs. Everyone listened respectfully, but doubtfully, because China was then not even in the auto race.

In 2012, China already dominated solar panels, but the Chevy Volt was the world’s most produced EV. No nation commanded battery production, which then was only nascently entering global competition.

Wu’s confidence in China’s capacity to deliver was well-founded. Today, nearly 70% of all new car sales in China are EVs, and half of all sales globally are Chinese-made electric vehicles. China produces around 80% of the world’s batteries and holds 70% of global battery patents. Its hosts half of the entire world’s large-scale battery storage capacity, primarily to store solar and wind power for the grid when the sun isn’t shining or the wind blowing.

As part of its whole-dragon approach, China also built out the widely distributed infrastructure of rapid charging stations across the country necessary to boost EV use. It launched a strategic push to link battery storage to the grid, requiring developers to build or commission large-scale storage capacity as a condition for approval of new wind or solar installations.

China’s export of its technology has enabled the advance of large-scale batteries for integration into power grids in many countries. Some 70% of EV batteries worldwide are from China.

California has the most installed large battery storage facilities outside of China. Its capacity has grown from a mere 700 megawatts in 2019 to 21,000 MW in 2026. By 2045, the state aims to reach 52,000 MW capacity to support a 100% clean energy grid. For the entire month of May 2026, 51% of California’s total energy demand came from solar power. Blackouts during the intense heatwaves of recent years have been avoided because the grid was linked to off-hour battery storage from renewable energy.

Though often assembled in California, 90% of the cells and core components of the large-scale batteries the state has installed come from China.

## **Quotas And Dumping**

From the standpoint of the race against time on climate, the widest possible dispersion of China’s green technology is a net plus for the planet. Yet, as in other realms of trade competition, its cheaper product and overproduction portends a vulnerable dependence on a political system which the West considers a strategic adversary.

To the extent domestic industries exist, China’s prowess threatens to run them out of business. Since green technology is critical to our future, the most sensible approach would not be to prohibit Chinese imports, but set a reasonable quota beyond which tariffs would kick in. That would both limit the damage while allowing competition from abroad to spark the scale-up of domestic industry.

Free-market ideologues aside, subsidies are not the end of the world when a livable biosphere is at stake. After all, up until the Trump administration, the U.S. did manage for a time to escape the pull of consumer immediacy. For years, it subsidized the purchase of EVs with tax rebates. And California has shown how regulation creates, not destroys, markets.Elon Musk’s Tesla empire would never have emerged if it were not for the state’s fuel efficiency and clean energy standards, which created the market for his technology.

> “Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China?”

## Is It Impolitic To Learn From China?

Given the urgency of addressing climate calamity, is it so impolitic to suggest that consumer democracies can learn something from China? This is not, of course, to imply in any way that the West turn toward autocracy or authoritarianism. It is only to warn that unless democracies can look beyond the short-term horizon and find ways to reach a governing consensus that sticks, they will be left in the dust of the oncoming future.

To turn an old Chinese saying toward ourselves: “The stones from hills yonder can polish jade at home.”

title: An Inside Look At How To Tame Unstoppable AI
content:
Credits

Anna August [specializes](https://annaaugust.com/) in AI governance, audit and compliance across the European Union, United Kingdom and Gulf Cooperation Council.

Earlier this year, a university decided to audit the effectiveness of its new AI system designed to help answer student questions. So, university officials hired me, an AI auditor, to come take a look. During my review, I discovered that the AI agent, which was supposed to handle only general questions about the academic calendar and organizational matters, had started opening students’ personal records —accessing data that wasn’t needed to answer their questions. The chatbot, however, did nothing further with that information.

When the university’s engineers, at the time, learned what happened from the access logs, they fixed it, and that was that. There was no official record. No internal rule required them to record such incidents, and nobody was assigned to track events like this. It was simply part of the engineering team’s bug-fixing process. The incident was what I call a near miss, and near misses are what a reporting system exists to catch. The same behavior could lead to something more serious next time, and we only know about this case because the university voluntarily brought me in to examine the system.

The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of high-risk systems to report serious incidents, and a chatbot that answers general questions is nowhere near that category. Even for high-risk systems, those duties do not apply until December 2027, and a near-miss that causes no harm would not count as a serious incident anyway.

That is why, as an AI auditor, I ask organizations at the start of every engagement to show me how they track system behavior through testing and deployment. I ask for records of systems acting in ways they’re not meant to, accessing data outside their role, anomalies and near-misses, or problems caught before they caused harm. Most places, like the university, have no such records.

The university had commissioned the audit voluntarily. There was no deliberate obfuscation of the facts on their part; there was simply no process to surface these important details, and nothing obliged them to build one, especially in the testing phase. Whatever an outsider learns about an AI system’s failures generally depends on the goodwill of the people who built it.

This summer showed the same gap on a larger scale. OpenAI’s test agents escaped their sandbox and broke into Hugging Face, and internal teams had seen warning signs for weeks before anyone outside the company found out. Anthropic then found intrusions of its own. By late September, OpenAI and Anthropic were reportedly investigating tens of thousands of incidents. Many have answered with calls for a pause. No company or country can afford to stop first, so the pause most likely will not come. But what can come is a real oversight, enforced and executed.

This essay argues for three requirements: registering frontier models before deployment, reporting incidents on a fixed legal clock, and independent audits that reach testing environments, not only released products. None of them asks anyone to slow down. In every country that adopts them, they put the race under independent observation. The goal is to make the race governed rather than left to voluntary restraint.

These days, the calls for a pause are coming from many different directions. In July, the Vatican and more than 200 Nobel Prize winners [called](https://globalnobelassembly.org/rome-declaration) for a global slowdown on artificial intelligence development. Soon after, more than 1,000 employees at top AI companies, along with managers at OpenAI and Anthropic, asked the American government to build a mechanism for a possible future pause. Then, over 3,000 economists, including AI researchers and Nobel Laureates, signed a [letter](https://www.wemustactnow.ai/), “We Must Act Now,” warning that the pace and scale of rapid artificial intelligence development could destabilize the economy and labor market faster than anyone is prepared for. And on 12 September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei [called](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) on frontier labs to “pace the frontier,” and OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis agreed within hours and days. That was a real catalyst for one of the most important discussions happening right now. Almost everyone weighed in, including Chinese politicians.

Alongside these pleas and letters, incidents at frontier companies this summer have created a genuine, ongoing crisis. Axios [reported](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/26/openai-anthropic-thousands-ai-security-incidents) that OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving potentially problematic model behavior, against a backdrop of hundreds of thousands of test runs conducted by AI companies.

> “Whatever an outsider learns about an AI system’s failures generally depends on the goodwill of the people who built it.”

## The ‘Confession’

The Hugging Face breach set off much of this summer’s soul-searching. And understanding its particulars is necessary to determine an appropriate solution. On July 21, OpenAI disclosed that its models had escaped a testing environment and broken into the systems of Hugging Face — a key platform that hosts much of the world’s open-source AI. Only a week later, Anthropic revealed that during testing, its models broke into the open internet and intruded into the systems of three separate organizations, extracting large production data from one of them. Both companies framed their announcements as the transparent, responsible thing to do, even if uncomfortable.

OpenAI had been running an evaluation of its models’ underlying cyber capabilities on a benchmark (called ExploitGym). Safety guardrails that would normally block the AI from proceeding were deliberately reduced, which is standard practice when testing a system’s safety. Some of the tasks were designed to be unsolvable. The models were supposed to be isolated from each other, each in its own sandbox, like students writing the same exam but in different rooms. But instead, more than 1,200 agents found a way to communicate through an internal message board. [They shared information](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/67869394-cb91-4c12-888c-5cbd85c7814c/OpenAI-Hugging-Face%20Incident-Technical-Report.pdf) about their tasks, goals, and, importantly, routes to the open internet. Within hours, they developed a universal cheat for the benchmark.

Over the next days, they [coordinated](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) the sustained effort to trick the scoring system into accepting their cheats. [More than 700 agents](https://www.redwoodresearch.org/research/hugging-face-incident#core-takeaways-about-this-incident) exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to reach outside OpenAI’s infrastructure on the open internet, inferred that Hugging Face might hold materials related to their evaluation, and broke into its production systems to steal what they expected would let them succeed on the test. If they were real-world students, they didn’t just cheat on the test; they broke into the teacher’s office to find the answer key.

Now, timing is critical and adds important context. It also makes the transparency framing more questionable. An internal OpenAI team observed agents using the message board and breaking into the open internet without authorization in late May. Another team found further evidence on June 27. On July 5, a message board outage triggered a formal security incident. The attack on Hugging Face took place between July 10 and 13 (by using exposed user credentials agents found on the internet). Hugging Face detected unauthorized activity in their production environments during the [week](https://huggingface.co/blog/agent-intrusion-technical-timeline) of July 13and reported the intrusion to the public and the police on July 16, not realizing it was a swarm of OpenAI’s test agents. OpenAI admitted it was them in the public disclosure on July 21. So the world learned about OpenAI’s misaligned agents only after Hugging Face made the story public and the police were already involved.

[Anthropic’s disclosure](https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals), published nine days later, was directly related to OpenAI’s reveal. As a result, Anthropic launched a retrospective review of its own cybersecurity evaluations and uncovered three previously undetected incidents, the earliest dating back to April 2026, in which its model gained unauthorized access to the systems of real organizations.

Since Hugging Face detected the intrusion on July 16 and reported it to police, the case has moved through several distinct phases, and the scope widened considerably in September. Reuters [reported](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/openais-rogue-agents-probed-hugging-face-weaknesses-two-months-before-major-hack-2026-09-16/) that OpenAI agents had probed Hugging Face and hijacked accounts as early as May, two months before the main attack, and the AI safety group Nightingale Collective [disclosed](https://collusion.wiki/) that agents had used a German wiki to coordinate their actions. On September 25, OpenAI [confirmed](https://openai.com/hugging-face-incident-and-misalignment/) a leak of more than 50 ChatGPT user images and said it had notified dozens of institutions, including universities and government agencies, of possible impact. In the same week, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese [revealed](https://www.news24.com.au/politics/australian-politics/watch-live-anthony-albanese-to-deliver-australias-national-statement-to-united-nations-general-assembly-in-new-york/news-story/cd39e1c15ac97bcede8ee5f83e0d8a3b) at the UN that an OpenAI agent had breached a government health portal in June.

On September 26, OpenAI [confirmed](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/tech-and-telecom-law/openai-says-its-models-may-have-interfered-with-government-sites) its agents had interacted with U.S. government sites including the Securities and Exchange Commission, the Census Bureau, and the Department of Education. On the same day, Axios reported that OpenAI and Anthropic are now investigating tens of thousands of security incidents, turning the Hugging Face case from a single episode into the opening chapter of a much larger crisis of control over autonomous AI agents.

> “A frontier company that discloses a containment failure, however big, is doing two things at once: admitting safety lapses and advertising its capabilities.”

But be mindful of this too: a frontier company that discloses a containment failure, however big, is doing two things at once: admitting safety lapses and advertising its capabilities. Every sentence describing how far the model reached, what defenses were defeated, how much initiative it showed, is simultaneously an incident report and a demo. Look how far our system got, even while we were trying to hold it back. Add public statements to the mix, and the contradiction becomes the story: you cannot plead for restraint and demonstrate you are winning the race in the same fortnight.

## What An Honest Incident Looks Like

To understand how flawed the current disclosure system has become, it’s worth looking at an AI incident with no press strategy attached. Because such incidents exist as well.

In August, in Australia, a man asked an AI agent to book him into a gym class. As the class was full, the man asked if the agent could move him up the waitlist. As a result, an agent canceled another member’s reservation by hacking the booking system. When asked to undo the change, it couldn’t restore the stranger’s booking. A person lost their gym slot to a machine that discovered, entirely unprompted, that the rules were optional (no authorization checks on cancellation). The story [surfaced](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-10/ai-assistant-hacks-gym-website-aus-cyber-attack/107007986?utm_source=chatgpt.com) because the user himself talked about it.

First, this small incident shows the same behavioral signature in miniature as the big laboratory breaches: an agent is given an objective, encounters a constraint and treats it as an engineering problem rather than a boundary. Breaking the rules was the shortest path to the goal, and nothing in their construction weighted the difference. This is why I believe escapes are closer to a default failure mode than a single event. Sandboxes and permission systems were designed to contain software that does what it is told. Agentic systems are built, as their central selling point states, to find routes around obstacles, to solve problems, to learn tendencies and act on them, rather than follow instructions. Testing it inside a container is asking it to solve the container, and occasionally it will.

Second, the gym incident shows what AI risk looks like when no one is filtering the disclosure. Staged laboratory disclosures are wrapped in lawyers, timing and framing. But accidental reports from users or victim police reports are a completely different story. Any reporting regime designed and operated by the AI companies themselves exposes the difference. Escapes are structurally likely, and this summer showed that containment did not fail for the first time. It reached a point where failures could no longer be hidden, intentionally or otherwise.

New York State Assemblymember Alex Bores used the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident to expose gaps in mandatory AI incident reporting. He argued that the initial version of the RAISE Act, or Responsible AI Safety and Education Act, a New York state law regulating frontier AI labs, would have required reporting such incidents to the New York Attorney General and the state’s Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services. But after lobbying from OpenAI, the reporting thresholds of how serious or risky an event must be before it must be reported to the state were raised so high that an event like the Hugging Face breach would no longer qualify for mandatory disclosure.

## Why Nobody Stops First

Incidents over the summer exposed internal oversight failures and a lack of timely, independent scrutiny. But is that a reason to slow down? To understand this, we must understand the nature of the race itself. Being part of a larger ecosystem gives no company the luxury of slowing down. Companies and their frontier AI labs cannot afford to fall behind rivals, so they are burning sums of capital unseen in prior human history to reach the verge of unstoppable capabilities. A pause would be a gift to competitors. The same logic also plays out between regions and countries; neither Washington nor Beijing will slow down because AI is a strategic asset and nobody wants to fall behind or suffer the consequences.

We have encountered this kind of moment in history before: The Cold War-era arms race between the United States and the Soviet Union is the closest example for a specific reason. It depended on the same concept — that technology could be leverage over the other, making unilateral restraint irrational for both. Both powers shared an interest in limiting competition (risks, costs, public opinion, etc.) and knew the best shared outcome was fewer weapons, but neither could safely restrain itself, as it would only strengthen the opponent and, in their view, look like surrender.

> “Agentic systems are built … to find routes around obstacles, to solve problems, to learn tendencies and act on them, rather than follow instructions. Testing it inside a container is asking it to solve the container, and occasionally it will.”

What eventually made meaningful arms-control agreements possible was not dialogue, pleas and protests alone. It was verification. Satellite reconnaissance, recognized and protected as a national technical means of [verification](https://doi.org/10.1080/01402390.2022.2161522) under the [SALT agreements](https://www.ruhr-uni-bochum.de/gna/Quellensammlung/11/11_salt1_1972.htm), made missile sites, launchers and related infrastructure increasingly observable. Later [agreements](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.4876454), particularly INF and START, added extensive data exchanges, notifications and on-site inspections. Verification did not end the arms race on its own. Political leadership, economic pressure and, above all, the transformation of Soviet policy under Mikhail Gorbachev, all played important roles. But verification was [critical](https://www.nationalacademies.org/projects/PGA-NETWORKS-20-01/publication/26558) in turning arms control from a collection of promises into a system of reciprocal, verifiable commitments. That was the game changer.

From this past example and from learning that unilateral restraint is irrational, relevant capabilities, safeguards and incidents must become independently observable. We already have tools that could form such a verification system. First, registration should be mandatory for frontier models before deployment, so that their understanding, scale and awareness are known to dedicated people outside the organization that builds them. Second, incident reporting should occur on a fixed clock — meaning there is a statutory deadline to report an incident to a regulatory body. That will allow us to move away from the communications team’s schedule and instead place it within the regulatory framework. Third, we need external audits, not only of the production systems, but of the testing environments themselves, which shows where the real danger is taking shape, as shown this summer.

As an AI auditor and someone who spent nearly 20 years working in IT, I know this territory well. So I also understand the instinctive response many in that world will give: “But what matters is the production environment!” Well, sure, that too. But we’re no longer talking about static software. We are talking about dynamic artificial intelligence. We need to stop treating AI like software development. It requires strict testing environments, like clinical trials. We do not begin regulating a medicine only once it reaches the market. We make sure the processes and testing that lead to a medication’s release on the market leave clear compliance records of its entire journey. Rigor in the testing environment is what will keep us safe.

All that this requires is granting visibility, but not visibility just through voluntary disclosure. While Anthropic’s unilateral proposal to invite independent evaluators in is helpful and even admirable, it is still the company’s voluntary choice, scoped to its own walls and revocable at will. This essay argues that independent external scrutiny should become a floor rather than a ceiling: a statutory cross-industry obligation that doesn’t depend on a single leadership team’s goodwill. This means the race runner isn’t being asked to lose the race or stop. Someone simply runs alongside him in the sunlight.

How might this have worked in the case of OpenAI and Hugging Face? First, if OpenAI had registered the model with regulators, they would have been aware of it before it was placed in evaluation with its safeguards reduced. Even simple facts, like that this class of model exists, are being tested and have a named accountable person overseeing their testing. Second, reporting at a fixed time would require reporting within days after the team noticed the anomalies in late May. It would be treated the same as the data breach already is under European law, rather than as an internal curiosity for over six weeks, during which the behavior only escalated. And third, an audit would ensure that the architecture evaluation, behavior and artifacts would be examined by someone who did not benefit from the evaluation finishing on schedule and according to the assumptions. Importantly, none of this requires changing the pace of the research. It only converts something currently private and constrained by goodwill into a fact external parties can see.

## Complementary Regulatory Regimes

Of course, all this is easy to say and hard to build. Indeed, building independent, publicly funded mechanisms may be challenging. But this process has already started in various countries. The problem is that each has some pieces of the puzzle but misses others. No nation is building a comprehensive system that captures the need holistically. A regulation’s ability to shape behavior depends entirely on enforcement, but every jurisdiction is going about it slightly differently.

> “We need to stop treating AI like software development. It requires strict testing environments, like clinical trials. We do not begin regulating a medicine only once it reaches the market.”

The European Union has arguably the most comprehensive AI regulatory framework to date. AI Act [obligations](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-101) for general-purpose models existed on paper in August 2025 and remained there — on paper — for an entire year until full enforcement powers became active this last August. The AI Office and national authorities can now impose fines of up to 15 million euros or 3% of a company’s total global annual revenue (whichever is higher). Now the question is whether a comprehensive law translates into real authority. The EU is quite bureaucratic, and it may be some time before we see real-world enforcement. For now, the question remains as to whether this extensive legal framework [translates](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/commission-decision-establishing-european-ai-office) into effective and timely enforcement in practice.

South Korea is similar. Its AI Basic Act, in force since January, also aims to be a single framework covering the technology rather than a product-safety regime added to existing market rules. Yet again, it operates under a grace period of at least one year, with the possibility of an extension, during which investigations and penalties are largely deferred (except for serious cases, such as serious social harm) to let industry adapt. So it’s similarly unclear whether the comprehensive law actually converts into real authority. Why are governments letting the market adapt itself? It might not have the anticipated effect — quite the opposite — the Wild West with no sheriff will not peacefully settle. Its inhabitants may simply no longer be able to distinguish good from evil. And if you add regulations that are binding but not enforced, you get [complete chaos](https://www.stimson.org/2026/south-koreas-ai-basic-act-seeking-balance-between-industry-innovation-and-social-risk/).

Then there is China. China [requires](https://www.chinatalk.media/p/sb-1047-with-socialist-characteristics) registration of certain generative AI services with the state before deployment and gives regulators access to models before the public sees them. Its oversight sits upstream, before release, bringing it closest to the laboratory door. The failure of that framework is unfortunately the intention. The purpose is sovereignty, not safety: the registry exists to ensure that AI primarily serves state interests — to protect the state from the people, not the people from the technology. It combines safeguards with content control, national security objectives and ideological requirements. What China demonstrates, however, is that pre-deployment control is technically and administratively possible.

The United States has a bill that covers part of this ground. The bipartisan [FRONTIER Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/9925/text), introduced in July and still in committee, would require frontier developers to report a critical safety incident within 72 hours, the fixed clock I argue for. It would also require the largest developers to hire an independent verifier licensed by the Department of Commerce, with access to company records, personnel and systems and with the internal use of models inside its scope. In mid-September, [OpenAI said](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/15/openai-backs-bipartisan-house-plan-for-third-party-safety-assessments-01076588) it supports the audit provision, though not the bill as a whole. As with the other regimes, pieces are missing: registration covers companies, but not each model, meaning regulators will know who is building frontier AI but won’t have a clear record of which models are actually being developed or deployed, and the text doesn’t specifically talk about testing environments.

These regulatory regimes have complementary frameworks that, on their own, have flaws, but collectively could offer a path forward: Europe’s independent institutions with real sanctioning powers, Korea’s comprehensive scope, America’s proposed 72-hour reporting clock and China’s pre-deployment reach, redirected from state control to public safety. What we see here is not a lack of invention. It’s a gap of assembly, and assembly is a political task, not a technical one. And that matters enormously, because a movement can spend the energy of its Nobel laureates on assembled enforcement rather than an unachievable pause.

## What Aviation Teaches Us

There is a saying that real oversight is often forced by catastrophe, and that this oversight can strangle what it touches. Aviation is a great example of both. It is the strongest evidence we have that regulation can help, and the parallel runs deeper than black boxes.

When commercial aviation began, it was all that AI is now: a glamorous, vital industry, racing toward competitiveness, regulating itself and treating accidents as private matters. It became the safest complex system humanity has ever operated. This result came from building four interlocking mechanisms. Each maps perfectly onto today’s AI landscape.

> “When commercial aviation began, it was all that AI is now: a glamorous, vital industry, racing toward competitiveness, regulating itself and treating accidents as private matters.”

The first is an independent investigator. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) investigates civil aviation incidents in the United States, and it’s clear and important that it has no stake in the outcome. The NTSB doesn’t regulate airlines, license pilots, or answer to industry leaders. The only product of its activity is getting to the truth of what happened. No such equivalent exists in the AI world. The METR/Redwood investigations of the Hugging Face incident were valuable, but they were also the result of an agreement with OpenAI that the company scoped; OpenAI determined what access it got and to which records. Imagine that scenario in an air crash inquiry.

The second is mandatory reporting of all incidents, not just disasters. It quickly became clear that crashes are the visible tail of a long distribution of near-misses, and that learning lives there. Everybody, from pilots to controllers to mechanics, must (and is crucially enabled to) report anomalies that may not yet have harmed anyone. As we saw this summer, in AI it’s the opposite — a two-month trail of internal warning signs at OpenAI, none required anyone to report, and this only surfaced after Hugging Face, the victim, reported it to the police. An aviation-style regime would have required the company to report the late May anomalies and would have prevented agents from engaging in many more weeks of malicious activity.

The third is a black box. Its goal is to remove the possibility of unrecorded failure that cannot also be simply rewritten after an event. Because of that, there is no such thing as an accident where the facts belong only to the airline. AI’s equivalent could be tamper-evident logging of training and evaluation runs, kept outside of the company’s own control. The Hugging Face incident shows the danger exactly — the agents had also tried to tamper with the logs recording them. Proof of that would also be visible in the black box.

And finally, the fourth mechanism might be the least understood outside the industry and the most important: a no-blame reporting culture. Aviation safety improved dramatically when reporting an error was separated from punishment. Since 1976, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration has maintained the voluntary Aviation Safety Reporting System, which allows pilots, controllers and maintenance personnel who confess a mistake to feed the learning system instead of ending their careers. It also protects reporters from enforcement rather than exposing them. This scheme receives more than 100,000 reports per year, and the safety literature it has created is enormous and has helped aviation workers learn from events that harmed no one.

The current AI disclosure policies invert every aspect of that design. This summer, there was silence until silence became untenable; then came the lawyers and the whole machinery of reputational events. In aviation it worked because it made the routine disclosure cheap and concealment expensive. Of course, it’s not a blanket of immunity — protection doesn’t follow deliberate conduct or criminal accidents. The goal is to distinguish between an honest error and reckless or willful misconduct. Engineers who flag anomalies should be protected, while companies that ignore repeated warnings or go against reporters should be held accountable.

In aviation, almost every element of the system is visible, reported and accountable. The example above shows that when human safety is at risk, there is no room for shortcuts or nonchalant behavior.

## The Counterarguments

Two common counterarguments deserve a reply. First, oversight can be expensive, and it’s true that it will land more lightly on well-resourced companies that can afford it. This means that governance could strengthen the largest labs that can afford to comply and dominate the market. However, this is not a reason to abandon oversight. In fact, it’s an argument against companies organizing and paying for their own audits. An alternative to this would be a publicly funded oversight body like the NTSB. This would enable a competitive market subject to meaningful oversight.

> “In aviation, almost every element of the system is visible, reported and accountable. … When human safety is at risk, there is no room for shortcuts or nonchalant behavior.”

The second counterargument is that the proposed oversight measures do not reduce the underlying risk attached to increasingly powerful AI systems; it only allows us to observe the risk and respond to incidents. According to some, knowledge doesn’t guarantee safety, and the only option is a slowdown to address the underlying danger of building systems more capable than our ability to contain them. But that remedy is unrealistic and likely unavailable. Individual restraint is irrational; collective restraint requires coordination machinery that doesn’t exist, and such machinery cannot be built among rivals without a mandated public reporting regime. In the same way verification worked to defuse the arms race many decades ago, visibility was the precondition for it. Any future negotiated pause between Washington and Beijing will happen only because registration, reporting and inspection exist to make it possible. It is the only path that lets societies, companies and governments fulfill the vision of a safe and secure future, with humans at the center and supported by AI at its best.

The pace of AI is not a variable anyone can realistically control right now, and demanding that it slow down is like asking a river to change its current. But what we can control is whether the most consequential technology of the century continues to be developed in the dark, with its failures surfacing through victim interviews and police reports. This summer showed us exactly what was missing in unregulated company testing rooms where agents organized themselves, cheated, tampered with their logs and hacked another company while warnings went by unnoticed. It’s not about forcing people to slow down; it’s about ensuring that no one runs the race without oversight. And unlike the plea for a pause, it is achievable — and, most importantly, doesn’t require the racer’s consent. It requires independent scrutiny, enforcement and visibility.
